title: YOZZ: Zero-knowledge webmail
pitch: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️.
about_excerpt: 🗿 Browser decrypt; server no key. WebMCP only way for 🤖. Server MCP cannot 🙅‍♀️. Like 1 Comment Story Updates YOZZ's three-pane inbox with multiple email addresses and a message open Inspiration YOZZ started with a personal problem. For years, I relied on Gmail’s “Send as” feature to send emails from my custom domains. When Google announced it was discontinuing the feature , I went looking for an alternative. After days of searching, I was unable to find anything that satisfied the privacy, aesthetics, and convenience that I was after. That is why I built YOZZ: a zero-knowledge, modern-looking webmail client that is private by design, clean to use, and accessible anywhere in the browser. Zero-knowledge password managers were the main inspiration for YOZZ: secrets are decrypted on the user’s device while the servers only handle data it cannot understand. What if I apply the same idea to webmail? Modern email interfaces and zero-knowledge cryptography were well-established and easy to learn from existing solutions. The real challenge lay in the networking: client-side JavaScript cannot open raw TCP sockets, so a direct connection to mail servers via IMAP/SMTP is impossible. Moving the connection to a backend server would defeat the whole zero-knowledge premise. The entire feasibility of YOZZ came down to whether I could solve that one fundamental constraint. Having previously built a zero-dependency ACME client in TypeScript, I knew low-level cryptographic handshakes were viable in pure JS. The missing link was the transport layer. The breakthrough was a Cloudflare Worker acting as a relay: tunneling WebSocket traffic from the browser into raw TCP connections to the mail servers, while ensuring TLS terminated exclusively between the JS in the browser and the mail servers. The worker sees only encrypted bytes. Once that proof-of-concept held up, I knew the architecture was sound. YOZZ has since become the daily driver for all my custom-domain email. The biggest capability YOZZ lacked was AI assistance. Moving my daily email workflow from Gmail to YOZZ made that clear: I had grown used to Gemini inside Gmail and to ChatGPT’s Gmail connector for more complex tasks spanning my other connected services. I first considered connecting YOZZ to ChatGPT through a conventional connector or server-side MCP. But YOZZ’s service has no readable access to mailbox credentials or mail, and giving it that access would break the product’s zero-knowledge premise. I also tested local models through Transformers.js, but the models I tried were either not reliable enough for work as sensitive as email or too slow and resource-hungry on my hardware. When this challenge introduced me to WebMCP, I realised that a capable external agent could instead work through the user’s active YOZZ client. What it does YOZZ is a zero-knowledge webmail client for supported IMAP and SMTP accounts you already own. Its server-side infrastructure receives no plaintext mailbox credentials or messages. Received mail remains with the existing provider and is cached only on the user’s device. Credentials, drafts and any sent-mail copies stored on the server are encrypted by the web app before reaching D1. YOZZ’s web app and the mail provider are the TLS endpoints. Since browser APIs cannot open the required TCP connections to mail servers, the relay simply forwards the ciphertext between them. It never receives the TLS session keys, mailbox passwords or plaintext messages, so YOZZ’s server-side infrastructure cannot decrypt the traffic it carries. This boundary is deliberately narrow. The existing mail provider retains its access, and an external agent can read mail returned through WebMCP. The user chooses which agent receives that mail; YOZZ’s servers gain no readable access in either case. YOZZ does retain limited operational metadata. “Zero-knowledge” here applies to stored vault contents and traffic crossing the relay. It does not make email end-to-end encrypted or protect against malicious client code delivered to the browser. After the user logs in, YOZZ registers six focused WebMCP tools: get_addresses : list the configured addresses. get_threads : search and read conversations without marking them as read. update_threads : mark conversations read or unread, star them, archive them or move them to Trash. save_draft : create a message, prepare a reply or update an existing draft. delete_draft : discard a draft, recoverable for 30 days. navigate : open a conversation or draft in the interface. Opening an unread conversation marks it read, just like the user’s own click. navigate is the only tool that changes what the user is currently looking at. The other tools work in the background without taking the user away from their current task. Before WebMCP, every multi-message task had to be completed manually inside YOZZ. Now the user and agent can divide the work: the agent can summarise unread mail across every configured address, find messages about a trip or purchase, clean up selected low-value threads and prepare a reply. The resulting draft can be opened inside YOZZ for review, but no WebMCP tool can send mail . Sending is a separate action in YOZZ's visible composer. A browser-capable agent may offer to perform that action, but only after surfacing the draft and requesting the user's confirmation. Why WebMCP belongs here For these workflows, a conventional server-side MCP integration would require moving readable mailbox access from the web app into server-side infrastructure, breaking YOZZ’s zero-knowledge premise. It would need mailbox credentials, an equivalent authorisation token or a server-terminated mail session. Any of those would give YOZZ’s infrastructure readable mailbox access it deliberately does not have. WebMCP instead uses the capabilities already present in the user’s logged-in web app, allowing an agent chosen by the user to work with mail without giving YOZZ’s servers new access. The immediate audience is people who already use custom-domain email or other IMAP and SMTP accounts and want webmail without entrusting another client operator with their credentials. YOZZ supports multiple inbound and send-only addresses, and Google’s upcoming change gives some of these users a concrete reason to seek another client. How I built it YOZZ is a deployed TypeScript application whose server-side infrastructure runs on Cloudflare Workers. Its web app implements TLS 1.3, X.509 certificate validation, IMAP, SMTP and MIME message handling. The API Worker handles three things: User authentication. Storing and updating ciphertext vault records in D1, including records for mailbox credentials, drafts and sent-mail copies. All are encrypted by the web app before reaching the Worker. The WebSocket-to-TCP relay. video_transcript_excerpt: Hello, I'm Jason. I built a zero-knowledge webmail client called Yoz. Zero-knowledge roughly means the servers can't see your stuff. So, how is Yoz zero-knowledge? When you save sensitive data, your browser encrypts it right there on your machine before sending it off. Yoz's servers only ever store and return scrambled unreadable ciphertext. We don't hold the key and we can't see what's inside. For example, this API response contains my saved mail account, but the actual details are returned as ciphertext. Only the unlocked web app can turn that ciphertext back into something meaningful, in this case, the email address you see here. Mail traffic follows the same principle. The TLS connection runs between the Yoz web app in your browser and the mail server you use. Yoz's relay only transports encrypted traffic. The session keys exist at those two endpoints, so the relay cannot decrypt what passes through it. In short, Yoz's servers are blind. We cannot read your mail. So, how can Yoz connect with AI agents? A traditional server-side MCP is impossible because Yoz's servers are blind, cannot read mail. So, we need something that works purely on the client side that also connects to AI. Wait a second. Isn't this exactly what web MCP's for? Let's see this in action now. Here, I have Yoz open in ChatGPT desktop. Yoz registers six web MCP tools directly with the page. I give ChatGPT a simple request to summarize the inbox. ChatGPT gives me a clear summary of the mailbox. Notice how it also flags the suspicious confirm your mailbox email. Yoz marks tools that return mail as carrying untrusted content. This tells the agent to treat what it reads with caution. By design, every tool except one works in the background. So, you can use Yoz while the agent is working. The one exception is the navigate tool, which is used when the agent needs to show you something for review. Let's ask ChatGPT to reply to Sam about the lunch. It saves the reply as a draft, then uses the navigate tool to open the draft editor in Yoz. Now, I can review the message and press send myself. Together, these tools let your agents read, organize, and draft mail through the unlocked web app without giving Yoz's servers any new access. That is how Yoz brings capable AI to your mailbox without giving up its zero knowledge design.
